pos: n. (proper name; second son of Gomer, son of Japheth)
etymology: Hebrew Riphath, of uncertain meaning. The margin of 1 Chronicles 1:6 notes or, Diphath as it is in some copies, a difference of one Hebrew letter.
biblical_def: Riphath is named twice, both times in a list: “And the sons of Gomer; Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah” (Genesis 10:3), repeated at 1 Chronicles 1:6. He is a grandson of Japheth and the brother of Ashkenaz and Togarmah, which places his descendants among the northern peoples the prophets locate beyond Israel's horizon. The Authorized Version's margin at 1 Chronicles 1:6 is honest about the textual situation: some copies read Diphath, the Hebrew resh and daleth differing by a stroke. The dictionary records that without alarm; the Masoretic tradition preserves both readings and nothing doctrinal turns on either. What matters is the chapter he stands in. Genesis 10 is the genealogy of the whole human race from one man and his three sons, and it is the Bible's answer to every theory that makes the nations separately originated. “And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth” (Acts 17:26). Riphath is a name and nothing more to us; he is a father of nations in the only account of human origins God has given.

corruption_summary: The Table of Nations is widely treated as late ethnographic myth; Scripture gives it as the genealogy of the one human race.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 10 is routinely handled as a post-exilic schematisation of the known world rather than as Mosaic record. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and the historicity of Noah and his three sons. The chapter is not a map of what Israel happened to know; it is the account of how the nations came to be, and the apostle preaches it at Athens as fact.

The principle to recover is the unity of the race. One blood, one Adam, one flood, one family of Noah — which is why Scripture knows nothing of autonomous racial categories and why every man is a neighbour and a kinsman. Riphath's descendants and Israel's share a great-grandfather.

pos: n. (proper name; second son of Joktan, of the line of Shem)
etymology: Hebrew Sheleph, from a root meaning to draw out. The name survives in southern Arabian tribal geography.
biblical_def: Sheleph appears twice, in the same clause both times: “And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah” (Genesis 10:26), repeated verbatim at 1 Chronicles 1:20. He belongs to the line of Shem through Eber and Joktan, and Joktan's thirteen sons are the Arabian branch of the Shemite family — Hazarmaveth is Hadramaut, and the others are traceable to south Arabian peoples. The Authorized Version keeps the list intact in both places. The dictionary notes that this is the line that matters most in Genesis 10, because Shem is the son through whom the promise runs: Eber gives his name to the Hebrews, and Eber's other son Peleg carries the line toward Abraham. Sheleph is in the branch that goes aside. Scripture names him anyway, which is the whole character of biblical genealogy — the branches that do not carry the covenant are still recorded, because God is the God of all the families of the earth and not only of the elect line.

corruption_paragraphs: The only handling worth answering treats the Shemite genealogy as a retrospective charter for Israel's claims rather than as record. Genesis 10 names Joktan's thirteen sons, most of whom have nothing to do with Israel, and names them with no polemical purpose at all. A charter does not bother with Sheleph.

Peleg carried the covenant line; Joktan's sons went to Arabia; and the Holy Spirit wrote down both lists, because the promise to Abraham was that in him all the families of the earth should be blessed.

pos: n. (proper name; fifth son of Cush, son of Ham)
etymology: Hebrew Sabtecha, of uncertain meaning; 1 Chronicles 1:9 spells it the same while the neighbouring Sabtah appears as Sabta.
biblical_def: Sabtecha closes the list of Cush's sons: “And the sons of Cush; Seba, and Havilah, and Sabtah, and Raamah, and Sabtecha: and the sons of Raamah; Sheba, and Dedan” (Genesis 10:7), with the parallel at 1 Chronicles 1:9. Cush is the first-named son of Ham, and his line spreads into Africa and Arabia; Seba and Sheba and Dedan are names the prophets and the psalms use of distant trading peoples who will one day bring gifts to Zion. The Authorized Version uses Sabtecha twice and tells us nothing else about him. The dictionary notes what the surrounding names make of the list. Cush's line includes Nimrod, the first empire-builder, three verses later; it also includes the peoples of Psalm 72:10, “the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts.” The same genealogy holds Babel and the nations who bring tribute to the Messiah. That is the shape of the whole Bible in one chapter: out of the families of the earth God raises both the tower and the worshippers.

corruption_summary: The genealogy of Ham has been abused to justify racial subjugation; Scripture gives no such warrant and the curse fell on Canaan.
corruption_paragraphs: The line of Ham has carried one of the ugliest misreadings in the history of interpretation. The curse of Genesis 9 fell on Canaan, not on Ham and not on Cush, and it was fulfilled in the Canaanite nations dispossessed under Joshua. It has never had anything to do with the peoples of Africa, and the use of this genealogy to justify enslaving them was wickedness built on a text that does not say it.

The principle to recover is Psalm 72:10. Cush's line is named among the peoples who bring gifts to the Messiah's throne, and the Ethiopian eunuch is reading Isaiah in Acts 8. In Christ there is neither Greek nor Jew, and the Table of Nations is a genealogy of one race, not a ranking of several.

pos: n. pl. (proper name; a people descended from Mizraim, son of Ham)
etymology: Hebrew Naphtuchim, a plural gentilic form, probably naming a district of Egypt. The -im ending marks a people rather than an individual.
biblical_def: The Naphtuhim appear twice: “And Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim” (Genesis 10:13), repeated at 1 Chronicles 1:11. Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt, and every one of his named sons is a plural — Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim. These are not individuals but peoples or districts, and the Authorized Version prints the plural forms as the Hebrew gives them. The dictionary notes the method of Genesis 10. The chapter moves freely between a man and a nation, because in the Hebrew way of reckoning a people is its father extended through time. That is not loose writing; it is the same logic by which the whole race is “in Adam,” and by which Levi is said to have paid tithes in Abraham before he was born (Hebrews 7:9-10). Federal headship is not a theological construction imposed on Scripture; it is the way Scripture counts. The Naphtuhim are a district of Egypt and a son of Mizraim at once, and the Bible sees no difficulty in that.

The same way of counting that makes the Naphtuhim both a man and a nation is what makes the covenant of works and the covenant of grace intelligible.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the eleven Canaanite peoples descended from Canaan)
etymology: Hebrew Sini, a gentilic from an unidentified place-name Sin. Not connected with Sinai, nor with the Wilderness of Sin.
biblical_def: The Sinite is named once in each of the two parallel lists: “And the Hivite, and the Arkite, and the Sinite” (Genesis 10:17), with 1 Chronicles 1:15. Canaan's descendants are eleven peoples — Sidon and Heth first, then the Jebusite, Amorite, Girgasite, Hivite, Arkite, Sinite, Arvadite, Zemarite, and Hamathite. These are the nations Israel was commanded to dispossess, and the Sinite is one of the five whose territory is never again mentioned. The Authorized Version prints the name and passes on. The dictionary notes what the list establishes. The conquest of Canaan was not an arbitrary land-grab; Genesis 15:16 says Abraham's seed would wait four hundred years because “the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full,” and Leviticus 18 catalogues what filled it. God named these peoples in Noah's generation, bore with them for centuries, and judged them at last through Joshua. A nation that vanishes from the record without a single narrative of its own is still a nation God numbered, warned, and dealt with justly.

corruption_summary: The conquest of Canaan is widely charged as ethnic cleansing; Scripture presents it as delayed judgment on named and warned peoples.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern charge against Joshua is genocide, and it is made without reference to what Scripture actually says about the Canaanites. Genesis 15:16 has God waiting four generations because their iniquity was not yet full; Leviticus 18 lists what filled it; Rahab shows that any Canaanite who feared the LORD was received, and she is in the genealogy of Christ. Judgment deferred for centuries and executed on moral grounds is not what the word cleansing means.

The principle to recover is the patience of God toward nations He eventually judges. He named the Sinites in Noah's generation and gave them four hundred years. The same patience is now extended to the nations of the earth, and the same judgment is appointed.

pos: n. (proper name; third son of Simeon)
etymology: Hebrew Ohad, of uncertain meaning, possibly connected with a root for union.
biblical_def: Ohad is named twice and only in the Simeonite list: “And the sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanitish woman” (Genesis 46:10), repeated at Exodus 6:15. He went down into Egypt with Jacob. What makes his name worth an entry is what happens to it afterwards: when Numbers 26 takes the census of Simeon's families in the wilderness, Ohad is gone. Nemuel, Jamin, Jachin, Zerah, and Shaul give their names to families; Ohad gives his to none. His line died out between Egypt and Sinai. The Authorized Version records him faithfully in both early lists and does not pretend he founded anything. The dictionary draws the plain lesson. Scripture keeps the names of men whose line failed, which no human chronicler bothers to do; and Simeon, the tribe Ohad belonged to, was itself the tribe Jacob cursed for the slaughter at Shechem and the tribe that all but disappeared into Judah. God's record is more honest than any family's own.

pos: n. (proper name; firstborn son of Zebulun)
etymology: Hebrew Sered, from a root meaning to escape or survive. The family formed from him is called the Sardites.
biblical_def: Sered is the firstborn of Zebulun: “And the sons of Zebulun; Sered, and Elon, and Jahleel” (Genesis 46:14). Unlike Ohad of Simeon, his line held, and the wilderness census records it: “Of the sons of Zebulun after their families: of Sered, the family of the Sardites” (Numbers 26:26). The Authorized Version uses the name twice, once at the descent into Egypt and once at the mustering for Canaan, and the two verses are four hundred years apart. The dictionary notes what sits between them. A man named among seventy souls going down into famine becomes a family numbered in a national army coming up to inherit. That is the arithmetic Exodus 1 makes explicit: the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and the land was filled with them. Zebulun's portion fell in the north, and Isaiah would name it in a prophecy the gospel quotes: the land of Zebulun and the land of Nephthalim, where the people that sat in darkness saw great light. Sered's family lived where Christ first preached.

pos: n. (proper name; fourth son of Naphtali)
etymology: Hebrew Shillem, from shalam, to be complete or to requite — the root behind shalom, peace, and shillem, recompense.
biblical_def: Shillem closes the list of Naphtali's sons: “And the sons of Naphtali; Jahzeel, and Guni, and Jezer, and Shillem” (Genesis 46:24). His line survived the sojourn, and Numbers records the family: “Of Jezer, the family of the Jezerites: of Shillem, the family of the Shillemites” (Numbers 26:49). The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes the root, which is worth more than the man's biography, since no biography exists. Shalam means to be whole, to be at peace, and therefore also to pay back in full — the same root gives shalom, peace, and the verb for making restitution in the law of trespass. Peace and recompense are one word in Hebrew because peace is what exists once the debt is fully paid. That is not etymological decoration; it is the logic of the atonement. “The chastisement of our peace was upon him” (Isaiah 53:5). A Naphtalite whose name means recompense-and-peace stands in the book of Genesis holding, without knowing it, the shape of the gospel.

Hebrew says peace and payment with one word, and Isaiah 53:5 says the chastisement of our peace was upon Him. There is no peace with God that is not a paid peace, which is why substitutionary atonement is not one theory among several but the thing the word itself means.

pos: n. (proper name; third son of Gad)
etymology: Hebrew Shuni, of uncertain meaning. The family formed from him is called the Shunites.
biblical_def: Shuni is named twice, both times in a Gadite list: “And the sons of Gad; Ziphion, and Haggi, Shuni, and Ezbon, Eri, and Arodi, and Areli” (Genesis 46:16), and in the census, “of Shuni, the family of the Shunites” (Numbers 26:15). The Authorized Version's margin at Genesis 46:16 is unusually busy, offering Zephon for Ziphion, Ozni for Ezbon, and Arod for Arodi — the translators recording the forms the Numbers list uses, so that the reader can see the lists are of the same family. The dictionary notes that this marginal work is a mark of the translators' honesty, not of textual trouble. The tribe Shuni belonged to has a particular history. Gad asked for the land east of Jordan and got it, with the condition that his armed men cross over and fight for their brethren first (Numbers 32). They did, and Joshua sent them home commended. The Gadites in David's day were men of war whose faces were like the faces of lions. Shuni's family came of a tribe that kept its word.

pos: n. pl. (proper name; the one family of the tribe of Dan)
etymology: Hebrew Shuchami, the gentilic of Shuham, who is called Hushim at Genesis 46:23 — the same man with the consonants transposed.
biblical_def: Dan's whole tribe descends from one man: “These are the sons of Dan after their families: of Shuham, the family of the Shuhamites. These are the families of Dan after their families” (Numbers 26:42). Every other tribe is counted in several families; Dan has exactly one. And it was enormous: “All the families of the Shuhamites, according to those that were numbered of them, were threescore and four thousand and four hundred” (Numbers 26:43) — the second largest tribe in Israel, from a single son. The Authorized Version uses Shuhamites in these two verses alone. The dictionary notes the pattern Scripture keeps setting. Dan had one son, Hushim or Shuham, and became 64,400 fighting men; the LORD multiplies from a narrow beginning as a matter of habit, from Abraham and Sarah onward. The tribe's later history is darker — Dan took Micah's graven image and his Levite, set up idolatry at Laish, and is missing from the sealed tribes of Revelation 7. A great family from one man is a mercy; what the family does with it is another matter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Shuhamites is a proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.
webster_full: Shuhamites is a Hebrew gentilic proper name; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.
The name appears at Numbers 26:42 and Numbers 26:43.
They are the single family of the tribe of Dan.
Their father Shuham is called Hushim at Genesis 46:23.
They numbered threescore and four thousand and four hundred in the wilderness.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hushim-Shuham difference is a favourite small exhibit for the documentary hypothesis. The consonants are the same and transposed, which in a Semitic name across four centuries and two scribal traditions is unremarkable; the Authorized Version prints both forms and the dictionary holds Mosaic authorship of both passages.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the two halves of Dan's story. From one son, 64,400 men — God multiplies from almost nothing. And then Judges 18, the stolen idol, the Levite for hire, the city renamed; the tribe that grew most is the tribe that fell furthest.
